claims.claim: Technology ethics is a branch of applied ethics that studies the moral questions raised by the design, development, use, and governance of technologies; computer and information ethics is characterized as an applied ethics that studies the social and ethical impacts of information and communication technology, similar to fields such as medical ethics and business ethics.

Design choices embody values: Langdon Winner argued that 'artifacts have politics' (1980) — some technologies embody specific forms of power and authority or are strongly compatible with certain social and political relations, and technologies may be political through the value system and structure of power reflected in how they were designed and deployed; value-sensitive design aims to integrate values of ethical importance into engineering design in a systematic way.
The value-neutrality thesis — that neither technology as such nor technologies or technical artifacts incorporate values — is a contested position in the philosophy of technology, not a settled fact.

The Collingridge dilemma (Collingridge 1980) holds that society's control over technological development is difficult because early in development there is higher control over outcomes but lower capacity to predict them, while later increased knowledge is accompanied by decreased control because the technology is more strongly embedded in society and investors and developers have vested interests; Collingridge proposed making innovation more corrigible and reversible and making developers and policymakers more accountable for technological choices.

Design cannot guarantee ethical outcomes: critics of 'ethics-by-design' note that the ethical ramifications of technologies depend not only on design but also on use, operation, maintenance, and retirement of the technology.

Data-collecting technologies can reduce individuals' control over their personal data and open the possibility of negative consequences; consent is an imperfect protection because consent requests interfere with task flows and users may simply click them away; surveillance and control concerns are documented in the literature, and collectors hold power over data subjects.

NIST research on bias in automated systems distinguishes statistical bias (prevalent in large-scale datasets), human bias (entering through data selection, curation, and annotation), and systemic bias (also called institutional or historical bias, rooted in institutional norms, practices, and history); fairness concerns are documented especially in consumer finance, housing, and employment.

Responsibility for harms from automated systems is difficult to assign because knowledge and control are distributed across many actors — the problem of many hands (Thompson 1980); the 'responsibility gap' (Matthias 2004) describes situations in which it may be difficult or impossible to hold humans blameworthy for the actions of learning automata, an account some philosophers dispute by reconceiving responsibility as distributed across human-technology collaborations.

Law and regulation lag behind technological change and vary across jurisdictions: NIST reports that there is currently no uniformly applied approach among regulators and courts to measuring impermissible bias, and the privacy literature describes declining clarity and agreement on privacy as giving rise to problems for law, policy, and ethics.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Do technologies embody values, or are they value-neutral?
positions: Value-neutrality thesis: neither technology as such nor technologies or technical artifacts incorporate values.
Critique (Winner 1980): artifacts have politics — technologies can embody specific forms of power and authority or reflect the values and power structures of their design and deployment.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Presented as a live dispute; the lesson attributes each position to its source and does not adjudicate between them.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Can ethics be guaranteed through design?
positions: Design-for-values and value-sensitive design aim to integrate values of ethical importance into engineering design systematically.
Criticism: the ethical ramifications of technologies depend also on use, operation, maintenance, and retirement, so design alone cannot guarantee ethical technology.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Both views attributed; the lesson presents design ethics as valuable but limited, per the SEP treatment.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Who is responsible when an automated system causes harm?
positions: Responsibility gap (Matthias 2004): for learning automata it may be increasingly difficult or impossible to legitimately hold humans blameworthy.

Alternative: responsibility gaps are better understood as responsibility distributed across collaborative human-technology agency, connected to the problem of many hands (Constantinescu and Kaptein 2025).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Both attributed and presented neutrally; the lesson uses the problem of many hands for its general analysis.

sourceRecords.title: Philosophy of Technology
sourceRecords.provider: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Metaphysics Research Lab, Stanford University
sourceRecords.notes: Read live (current edition, by Franssen, van de Poel, Klenk, and Santoni de Sio). Primary Tier A source. Supports: the value-neutrality thesis as a contested position; Winner's 'artifacts have politics' (Winner 1980); value-sensitive design (Friedman and Hendry 2019) and design-for-values; the criticism that design cannot guarantee ethical outcomes because consequences depend on use, operation, maintenance, and retirement; the Collingridge dilemma of control (Collingridge 1980) with its corrigibility/reversibility proposal; the problem of many hands (Thompson 1980); the responsibility gap (Matthias 2004) and the alternative distributed-responsibility account (Constantinescu and Kaptein 2025). Used for verification only; no prose reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Privacy and Information Technology
sourceRecords.provider: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Metaphysics Research Lab, Stanford University
sourceRecords.notes: Read live (entry first published 2014, substantive revision October 2024). Tier A source. Supports: technology's role in reducing control over personal data and opening negative consequences; consent as an imperfect protection because consent requests interfere with task flows and users click them away (citing Leenes and Kosta 2015); surveillance and control concerns and the term 'surveillance capitalism'; power asymmetries ('power over data subjects'); declining clarity and agreement on privacy giving rise to problems for law, policy, and ethics. Used for verification only; no prose reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Towards a Standard for Identifying and Managing Bias in Artificial Intelligence (NIST Special Publication 1270)
sourceRecords.provider: National Institute of Standards and Technology, U.S. Department of Commerce
sourceRecords.notes: Read the published NIST SP 1270 PDF (March 2022). Tier A standards-body source. Supports: the three categories of statistical, human, and systemic (institutional/historical) bias in automated systems; human bias entering through data selection, curation, and annotation; documented fairness concerns in consumer finance, housing, and employment; the statement that no uniformly applied approach among regulators and courts currently measures impermissible bias; governance and accountability as central to bias management. Used for verification only; no prose reproduced.
